items.title: AAIF Reading Group: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
Can forgetting help AI agents discover better solutions? And why do agents sometimes stop making progress, even when given more time, compute, and opportunities to experiment?

Join the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) community for an informal reading group exploring the paper “Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting.”

Paper: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2610.20563

Event page: https://home.mlops.community/public/events/aaif-reading-group-scaling-discovery-requires-forgetting-pg1zmi4qzx

In this session, Sparsh Jain walks us through the paper's approach to improving long-running discovery and research tasks by periodically resetting agent sessions and search history while preserving the best candidate discovered so far.

We'll explore how agents can become stuck in repetitive patterns, why simply adding more parallel agents or compute may not be enough, and how strategically forgetting previous attempts can help renew exploration and improve results.

This is not just about the paper's proposed approach. It's a community conversation about agent memory, context management, autonomous research, and the challenges of scaling agent systems in practice. Following the presentation, Arthur Coleman leads an open discussion, bringing in questions, practical experiences, and different perspectives from the community.

We'll explore:

Why AI agents plateau during long-running discovery and research tasks

How periodically resetting agent context can improve exploration and results

The role of parallel agents and collaboration in scaling discovery

What agents should remember, what they should forget, and when they should reset

The importance of memory reduction, evaluation, and context management

Practical challenges and limitations of applying this approach to real-world agent systems

If you've read the paper already, come ready to share your perspective. If you haven't, you're still welcome – we'll work through the ideas together.

Come curious. Bring questions. Let's explore whether sometimes, forgetting is exactly what makes AI agents better.

About the Agentic AI Foundation

The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is the open, neutral home for the agentic AI ecosystem, bringing together developers, researchers, companies, and communities to build open standards and infrastructure for interoperable AI agents.

items.title: What Happens When Engineers Stop Reading Their Own Code?
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
In this episode, we sit down with Matt Carey and Scott Crooks, engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself.

We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping.

The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about.

Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code.

Demetrios Brinkmann: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dpbrinkm
Matt Carey: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mattzcarey
